content: Honey is a thick, supersaturated sugar solution that is produced from nectar collected and processed by honeybees (Apis mellifera). It has been used since ancient times as a treatment for wounds. Research from animal studies and some clinical trials suggests that honey may promote faster wound healing. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effects of honey compared to other wound dressings and topical treatments in the healing of both acute wounds (e.g., burns, lacerations) and chronic wounds (e.g., venous ulcers). To update this review, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL, up to October 2014. Randomized and quasi-randomized trials that assessed honey as a treatment for any type of acute or chronic wound were included. There were no restrictions on the source, publication date, or language of the studies. The primary outcome of interest was wound healing. Data from eligible trials were extracted by one author and independently verified by another. Two additional authors reviewed the data for accuracy. A total of 26 trials involving 3,011 participants were included in the analysis. These trials examined the effects of honey on various types of wounds, including minor acute wounds, burns, venous leg ulcers, diabetic foot ulcers, infected post-operative wounds, pressure ulcers, cutaneous leishmaniasis, and Fournier’s gangrene. Some trials included mixed populations with both acute and chronic wounds. The quality of evidence varied across the studies and was often downgraded due to risks of bias, imprecision, and, in some cases, inconsistency. High-quality evidence from two trials (992 participants) demonstrated that honey dressings healed partial-thickness burns faster than conventional dressings, with a weighted mean difference (WMD) of -4.68 days (95% confidence interval [CI]: -5.09 to -4.28). However, there was very low-quality evidence regarding differences in adverse event rates or infection rates between honey and conventional treatments. For burns treated with honey compared to silver sulfadiazine (SSD), very low-quality evidence from four trials (332 participants) suggested faster healing with honey (WMD -5.12 days, 95% CI: -9.51 to -0.73). However, high-quality evidence from six trials (462 participants) indicated no significant difference in the overall likelihood of healing within six weeks between honey and SSD (relative risk [RR] 1.00, 95% CI: 0.98 to 1.02). Honey was associated with a lower risk of adverse events compared to SSD. Low-quality evidence from one trial (50 participants) suggested that early excision and grafting healed partialand full-thickness burns faster than honey followed by grafting as needed (WMD 13.6 days, 95% CI: 9.82 to 17.38). Additionally, low-quality evidence from two trials (140 participants) indicated that honey healed a mixed population of acute and chronic wounds faster than SSD or sugar dressings. Moderate-quality evidence from one trial (50 participants) showed that honey healed infected post-operative wounds faster than antiseptic washes followed by gauze, with fewer adverse events (RR of healing 1.69, 95% CI: 1.10 to 2.61). Very low-quality evidence from one trial (40 participants) suggested that honey healed pressure ulcers faster than saline soaks (RR 1.41, 95% CI: 1.05 to 1.90). Similarly, very low-quality evidence from one trial (30 participants) indicated that honey healed Fournier’s gangrene faster than Eusol soaks (WMD -8.00 days, 95% CI: -6.08 to -9.92). The effects of honey compared to other treatments were unclear for venous leg ulcers (two trials, 476 participants, low-quality evidence), minor acute wounds (three trials, 213 participants, very low-quality evidence), diabetic foot ulcers (two trials, 93 participants, low-quality evidence), cutaneous leishmaniasis (one trial, 100 participants, low-quality evidence), and mixed chronic wounds (two trials, 150 participants, low-quality evidence). In conclusion, the evidence regarding the use of honey as a topical treatment for wounds is limited and of varying quality. Honey appears to heal partial-thickness burns faster than conventional treatments (e.g., polyurethane film, paraffin gauze, soframycin-impregnated gauze, sterile linen, or leaving burns exposed) and infected post-operative wounds faster than antiseptics and gauze. However, for other wound types, the evidence is of low or very low quality, making it difficult to draw robust conclusions or make definitive recommendations.
